Mount Pelée. An active stratovolcano on the Caribbean island of Martinique, Mount Pelée is infamous for its devastating eruption in May 1902. The eruption destroyed the city of Saint-Pierre, known as the Paris of the West Indies, killing approximately thirty thousand people in minutes, making it the deadliest volcanic disaster of the twentieth century. The event revolutionized modern volcanology by demonstrating the speed and destructive power of pyroclastic flows. Only a few survivors remained, most famously Ludger Sylbaris, a prisoner who survived the superheated gas because he was locked in a poorly ventilated, semi-subterranean stone jail cell. The eruption popularized the study of pyroclastic flows, which were described in detail by French mineralogist Alfred Lacroix under the name nuée ardente, or glowing cloud. Following the eruption, a massive volcanic spine grew from the crater floor, reaching a height of over one thousand feet before collapsing. The eruption occurred during a local election cycle, which led the governor of Martinique to discourage evacuation to prevent panic and ensure residents cast their votes. Mount Pelée connects to Vesuvius, whose seventy-nine AD eruption similarly wiped out populated Roman cities via pyroclastic density currents, and to Mount Saint Helens, a modern volcano that also experienced a destructive lateral blast and pyroclastic flows.
